questions.q: In the terminology used to describe a computer, what does the term 'software' refer to?
o: The physical devices such as keyboard, screen, mouse and disks
The instructions that command the computer to perform actions and make decisions
The processing units and memory chips inside the machine
The electrical power supply that runs the hardware
questions.e: Software is the set of instructions that command a computer to perform actions and make decisions, whereas hardware is the collection of physical devices (keyboard, screen, mouse, disks, memory, processing units).

questions.q: Which of the following is classified as computer hardware rather than software?
questions.e: Hardware refers to the physical devices that make up a computer, such as the keyboard, screen, mouse, disks, memory and CD-ROM. Instructions and program statements are software.

questions.q: Why can't people currently give computers orders in an ordinary natural language such as English?
o: Natural language cannot be typed on a keyboard
Computers today are not intelligent enough to understand natural-language orders, which are also ambiguous
Natural language has no grammar rules
Compilers refuse to accept natural language for security reasons
questions.e: Today's computers are not intelligent enough to understand orders given in natural language, and natural language is ambiguous (for example, 'The tourist saw the astronomer with the telescope' has multiple meanings), so a defined programming language is needed instead.

questions.q: The sentence 'The tourist saw the astronomer with the telescope' is used to illustrate which property of natural language?
questions.e: The sentence can mean the tourist used the telescope, or the astronomer had the telescope, so it demonstrates ambiguity, a reason natural language is unsuitable for instructing computers.

questions.q: A machine language instruction such as 10110101011001 is an example of which category of programming language?
questions.e: Machine language, expressed in binary and defined by the hardware design, is a low-level language. High-level languages are much more understandable to humans.

questions.q: What is the role of a compiler in the context of programming languages?
o: It executes machine language directly on the processor
It translates a high-level language into a lower-level (assembly/machine) language
It converts binary back into natural language
It reserves memory space for variables at run time
questions.e: A compiler translates a high-level language, which is more understandable to humans, into assembly/machine language that the hardware can process.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly lists the phases a C++ program passes through in a typical environment?
o: Compile, Edit, Link, Load, Preprocess, Execute
Edit, Preprocess, Compile, Link, Load, Execute
Preprocess, Edit, Compile, Load, Link, Execute
Edit, Compile, Preprocess, Execute, Link, Load
questions.e: The typical phases of a C++ program are, in order: Edit, Preprocess, Compile, Link, Load, and Execute.

questions.q: According to the recommended approach to learning programming, what should be done to a given problem before writing any code for it?
o: It should be coded as fast as possible in one attempt
It should be broken down into small pieces that are turned into pseudo-code
It should be memorised in full before starting
It should be converted directly into machine language
questions.e: The suggested method is to write a good description of the problem, break it into small pieces, turn those pieces into pseudo-code, decide how to integrate them, write the program for each piece, and finally integrate all pieces together.

questions.q: In the six-step problem-solving approach, what is done immediately after each small piece has been turned into pseudo-code and its integration mechanism decided?
o: The program for each piece is written and then all pieces are integrated together
The pseudo-code is translated into machine language by hand
questions.e: After breaking the problem into pieces, turning them into pseudo-code and deciding the integration mechanism, the next steps are writing the program for each piece and then integrating all the pieces together.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects the advice given about programming tools such as IDEs, editors and debuggers?
o: They write the program automatically for the user
They only provide help; they do not write the program themselves, so there is no shortcut to programming skill
They replace the need to understand fundamental concepts
questions.e: IDEs, editors, debuggers and other tools merely provide some help in writing a program; they do not write it themselves, and there is no shortcut to programming skills and experience.

questions.q: Which of the following is given as a reason many students are afraid of programming?
o: Programming is a different paradigm where you cannot touch the final output, only feel it
Programming has no practical use after graduation
questions.e: Reasons cited include the paradigm change (you work on something you cannot touch, only feel), peer pressure, a lack of understanding of fundamental concepts, and the time factor.

questions.q: A preprocessor directive such as #include <iostream> differs from an ordinary program statement in what way?
o: It must end with a semicolon
It does not need a semicolon to end it because it is part of the functioning body, not a program statement
It is ignored by the preprocessor
It can only appear inside main()
questions.e: #include is a preprocessor directive and part of the program's functioning setup rather than an executable statement, so it does not require a terminating semicolon; iostream is the header file concerning input/output.

questions.q: In #include <iostream>, what is 'iostream'?
o: A header file that concerns input/output in the program
The name of the main function
questions.e: In the directive #include <iostream>, #include is the preprocessor directive and iostream is a header file that basically concerns the input/output (I/O) in the program.

questions.q: What does the statement 'using namespace std;' indicate about a program's names?
o: It deletes all previously defined names
It shows that the program statements that follow are within the std namespace
It prevents any names from being used
It converts names into machine code
questions.e: A namespace reorganises certain defined names; outside the namespace they are unknown. 'using namespace std;' shows that the following program statements are within the std namespace.

questions.q: In a basic C++ program, what happens if there is no main() function?
o: The program runs starting from the first function defined
The program runs but produces no output
The compiler creates a main() automatically
questions.e: Execution is controlled by main(), which begins at its first statement and ends at 'return 0;'. If there is no main function, an error will be generated.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the statement 'return 0;' at the end of main()?
o: It sends the program back to the initial position from where it started
It prints the value 0 to the screen
questions.e: 'return 0;' is a compulsory statement that sends the program back to the initial position from where it was started, indicating the program ended.

questions.q: How are single-line and multi-line comments written in C++?
questions.e: Single-line comments begin with //, and multi-line comments are enclosed in /* */. Comments document programs and improve readability but are ignored by the compiler.

questions.q: What is the effect of comments on a C++ program when it is compiled?
o: They are converted to machine code
They are ignored by the compiler
questions.e: Comments document programs and improve program readability, but they are ignored by the compiler and have no effect on execution.

questions.q: Every ordinary C++ program statement must end with which character?
questions.e: A program statement is the fundamental unit that tells the computer to do something and always ends with a semicolon; if it is omitted, an error is generated.

questions.q: In a program that computes the average grade of 3 tests for a whole class, what is the process step that comes immediately after adding the three scores together?
o: Divide by three to get the average
questions.e: The process is: get three scores, add them together, divide by three to get the average, print the average, then repeat for the next student. Dividing by three follows the addition step.

questions.q: In the ATM withdrawal algorithm, what action is taken when the requested amount is greater than the current balance?
o: An error message is generated and control jumps to the final stop step
The balance is set to zero
questions.e: If the amount is greater than the current balance, the algorithm generates an error message and goes to the final step (return the ATM card and stop), rather than dispensing cash.

questions.q: A program reads three different integers 13, 27 and 14 and prints their sum, average and product. What value is printed for the average?
questions.e: For the integers 13, 27 and 14 the sum is 54 and the integer average is 54/3 = 18. The product 13*27*14 = 4914.

questions.q: For the three integers 13, 27 and 14, what is the product that the program prints?
questions.e: The product of 13, 27 and 14 is 13*27*14 = 4914; the sum is 54 and the average is 18.

questions.q: In programming, what is a 'variable'?
o: A value that can never be changed
A reserved space in memory used to store a value
A comment that documents the code
questions.e: A variable is a space in memory reserved to store a value; the space is held until the variable is no longer required.

questions.q: A variable is described by three important characteristics. Which set correctly lists them?
questions.e: A variable's three characteristics are its Type (how much memory it needs), its Name (which refers to the memory location), and its Value (the actual content it holds).

questions.q: Which characteristic of a variable determines how much memory it needs?
questions.e: The Type of a variable determines how much memory it needs. The Name refers to the memory location, and the Value is the actual content stored.

questions.q: In a scheme where a float occupies 32 bits and a char occupies 8 bits, how many bits does a variable of type 'double' occupy?
questions.e: A double stores floating-point data with a large fraction and occupies 64 bits, twice the 32 bits of a float, while a long int is 32 bits and a char 8 bits.

questions.q: In a scheme where a plain int occupies 16 bits and a double occupies 64 bits, what size is a 'char'?
questions.e: The text type char occupies 8 bits, the smallest of these types; a plain int is 16 bits, a long int and a float are each 32 bits, and a double is 64 bits.

questions.q: In a scheme where a plain int occupies 16 bits and a double occupies 64 bits, how many bits do a 'long int' and a 'float' each occupy?
questions.e: Both a long int and a float (floating-point data) occupy 32 bits, sitting between the 16-bit int and the 64-bit double.

questions.q: Which keyword is used to declare a floating-point variable with a large fraction that occupies 64 bits?
questions.e: The double keyword declares floating-point data with a large fraction, occupying 64 bits, whereas float occupies 32 bits.

questions.q: Why is the statement x = x + 1 valid in C++ even though it looks impossible in mathematics?
o: Because C++ ignores the left-hand side
Because '=' is an assignment operator, not an equality operator
Because x is automatically treated as zero
Because the statement is only a comment
questions.e: In C++ '=' is an assignment operator, meaning the value of the right-hand side is transferred into the memory location of the left-hand side, so x = x + 1 stores the incremented value back into x.

questions.q: Which keyword is placed before a variable's type to declare a value that cannot be modified, such as const double pi = 3.14?
questions.e: Constants are values that cannot be modified. To declare one, the keyword 'const' is written before the variable type, for example const double pi = 3.14.

questions.q: What is the difference between 'a' and "a" in C++?
o: 'a' is a value of type character, while "a" is a string of characters containing one character
'a' is a string and "a" is a character
questions.e: 'a' (single quotes) is a value of type char, whereas "a" (double quotes) is a string of characters that happens to contain one character; character constants use single quotes and strings use double quotes.

questions.q: A variable of type bool can hold which values?
questions.e: bool is short for Boolean; a Boolean value is either true or false, declared for example as 'bool old_enough;'.

questions.q: What is the result of casting the float value 3.14 to an int, for example with i = (int) f; where f = 3.14?
questions.e: Casting converts a value of one type into another. Converting the float 3.14 to an integer yields 3, because the remainder (fractional part) is lost.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes the manual (explicit) casting syntax using the static_cast form?
questions.e: Manual casting can be done with the explicit form static_cast<double>(intVar), which converts intVar to a double.

questions.q: What kind of data is stored in a 'string' variable, and what is required to use it?
o: Only single characters; no header needed
Non-numerical values longer than one character; the <string> header and std namespace are required
Only integers; the <cmath> header is required
Boolean values; the <iostream> header is required
questions.e: Strings store non-numerical values longer than a single character. Support comes from the standard string class, which requires including the <string> header and access to the std namespace.

questions.q: Which escape code represents a newline?
questions.e: \n is the newline escape code. \t is tab, \r is carriage return, and \b is backspace. All escape codes are preceded by a backslash.

questions.q: In the list of escape codes, what does \t represent?
questions.e: \t is the tab escape code. \n is newline, \v is vertical tab, \b is backspace, and \a is the alert (beep).

questions.q: Which escape sequence must be used to place an actual backslash character into a string?
questions.e: A single backslash is written as \\ (backslash-backslash), because a lone backslash begins an escape sequence. \a is the alert/beep and \b is backspace.

questions.q: In C++ operator precedence, which group of operators is evaluated before addition and subtraction?
questions.e: Multiplication, division and remainder (*, /, %) are performed first, from left to right, and only then are additions and subtractions (+, -) performed from left to right.

questions.q: What does the associativity of an operator specify?
o: Which operator has the highest precedence overall
The order in which operations of the same precedence are performed
How many operands an operator needs
Whether an operator can be overloaded
questions.e: Operator precedence controls the order in which operations of different precedence are performed, while associativity specifies the order in which operations of the same precedence are performed.

questions.q: Which symbol is the modulus (remainder) operator in C++?
questions.e: The five arithmetic operators are + (addition), - (subtraction), * (multiplication), / (division) and % (modulo/remainder).

questions.q: Which of the following is the correct set of relational and equality operators in C++?
o: eq, ne, gt, lt, ge, le
questions.e: The relational and equality operators are == (equal to), != (not equal to), > (greater than), < (less than), >= (greater than or equal to) and <= (less than or equal to).

questions.q: For the logical NOT operator, what are the results of !0 and !1?
questions.e: The logical NOT operator inverts its operand: !0 = 1 and !1 = 0.

questions.q: After the statement a = (b = 3, b + 2); using the comma operator, what value does a receive?
questions.e: The comma operator evaluates both expressions: b is set to 3, then b + 2 (which is 5) becomes the value assigned to a. So a = 5 and b = 3.

questions.q: Using the conditional operator, what does the expression 7 == 5 ? 4 : 3 return?
questions.e: The conditional operator returns result1 if the condition is true and result2 otherwise. Since 7 == 5 is false, the expression returns 3.

questions.q: Using the conditional operator, what does the expression 7 == 5 + 2 ? 4 : 3 return?
questions.e: Because 5 + 2 equals 7, the condition 7 == 7 is true, so the conditional operator returns result1, which is 4.

questions.q: What is the general format of the conditional (ternary) operator?
questions.e: The conditional operator has the format 'condition ? result1 : result2'; it returns result1 if the condition is true and result2 if it is false.

questions.q: What is a flowchart?
o: A table listing all program variables
A visual or graphical representation of an algorithm using blocks and arrows
A list of reserved words in C++
A compiled version of a program
questions.e: A flowchart is a visual/graphical representation of an algorithm; it uses a series of blocks and arrows, where the arrows represent the sequence in which operations are implemented.

questions.q: In a flowchart, what do the arrows represent?
o: The sequence in which the operations are implemented
questions.e: In a flowchart, each block represents a particular operation or step, and the arrows represent the sequence in which the operations are implemented.

questions.q: The increment operators ++ and -- are used to do what to a variable?
o: Increase or decrease its value (e.g. c++ is equivalent to c = c + 1)
questions.e: The increase and decrease operators ++ and -- add or subtract one; c++, c += 1 and c = c + 1 are all equivalent ways of increasing c by one.

questions.q: In C++, what is a 'stream'?
o: An object into which a program can insert characters or from which it can extract characters
A type of variable that stores decimals
questions.e: C++ uses the abstraction of streams to perform input and output on sequential media. A stream is an object where a program can insert or extract characters to/from it.

questions.q: Which header file must be included to make the standard input and output stream objects available?
questions.e: The standard C++ library includes the header file iostream, where the standard input and output stream objects (such as cin and cout) are declared.

questions.q: By default, to which device does the standard output object cout send data?
questions.e: By default the standard output of a program is the screen, and the C++ stream object defined to access it is cout.

questions.q: Which operator is used with cout to send data to the screen?
questions.e: cout is used with the insertion operator, written as << (two 'less than' signs), to insert data into the output stream.

questions.q: What is the difference between cout << "Hello"; and cout << Hello;?
o: They both print the word Hello
The first prints the text Hello; the second prints the content of a variable named Hello
The first causes an error; the second prints Hello
questions.e: Constant strings of characters must be enclosed in double quotes, so cout << "Hello"; prints the text Hello, while cout << Hello; prints the content of a variable called Hello.

questions.q: In the statement cout << "Hello, " << "I am " << "a C++ statement"; what does the repeated use of << demonstrate?
o: That cout can only be used once per line
That the insertion operator may be used more than once in a single statement
That each string needs its own semicolon
That << reverses the order of the strings
questions.e: The insertion operator << may be used more than once in a single statement, so the three strings are joined and printed as 'Hello, I am a C++ statement'.

questions.q: Which object handles standard input, and which operator is used with it?
questions.e: Standard input, usually from the keyboard, is handled by applying the overloaded extraction operator >> on the cin stream, followed by the variable that will store the extracted data.

questions.q: When does cin process the input typed at the keyboard?
o: Immediately as each character is typed
Only once the RETURN key has been pressed
Only when the screen is cleared
questions.e: cin can only process input from the keyboard once the RETURN key has been pressed, and the type of the receiving variable must always be considered.

questions.q: The statement cin >> a >> b; is equivalent to which of the following?
o: cin >> a; followed by cin >> b;
questions.e: cin >> a >> b; is equivalent to writing cin >> a; then cin >> b;. The user must supply two data items separated by a blank separator such as a space, tab or newline.

questions.q: When reading two values with cin, which characters can be used to separate the two inputs?
o: A space, a tab character, or a newline
questions.e: When requesting more than one datum, the user separates them by any valid blank separator: a space, a tab character or a newline.

questions.q: In the two-integer addition program, if the user enters 45 and then 72, what is printed as the sum?
questions.e: The program stores 45 in integer1 and 72 in integer2, computes sum = integer1 + integer2 = 117, and prints 'Sum is 117'.

questions.q: To always display a fixed number of decimal places (for example two), which member function specifies the number of digits after the decimal point?
questions.e: precision(2) specifies that two decimal places will always be shown; setf(ios::fixed) selects fixed-point notation and setf(ios::showpoint) forces the decimal point to always appear.

questions.q: Which setting specifies fixed-point notation for floating-point output?
questions.e: setf(ios::fixed) specifies fixed-point notation; setf(ios::showpoint) ensures the decimal point is always shown, and precision(2) sets the number of decimal places.

questions.q: When cin is used with the extraction operator >> to read a string, why can it capture only one word at a time?
o: Because strings can hold only one word
Because cin extraction stops reading as soon as it finds any blank space character
Because >> only reads the first character
questions.e: cin extraction stops reading as soon as it finds a blank space character, so only one word is captured per extraction; getline is recommended to read whole lines.

questions.q: Which function is recommended to read an entire line of input, including spaces, into a string with cin?
questions.e: Because cin >> stops at the first blank space, the function getline is the recommended way to get an entire line of user input into a string.

questions.q: What capability does the <sstream> header provide?
o: It allows a string-based object to be treated as a stream, useful for converting strings to numbers and vice versa
It provides mathematical functions like sqrt
questions.e: The standard header <sstream> allows a string-based object to be treated as a stream, so extraction/insertion can be performed on strings, which is especially useful for converting strings to numerical values and back.

questions.q: A block (compound statement) in C++ is best described as what?
o: A single statement without a semicolon
A group of statements grouped together and enclosed in braces { }
questions.e: A block, or compound statement, is a group of statements (each ending with a semicolon) grouped together and enclosed in braces { }, for example { statement1; statement2; statement3; }.

questions.q: C++ provides three kinds of control structures. Which option lists them correctly?
questions.e: The three control structures are the sequence structure (executed by default), selection structures (if, if/else, switch) and repetition structures (while, do/while, for).

questions.q: Which control structures are the selection structures in C++?
questions.e: The selection structures are if, if/else and switch. while, do/while and for are the repetition structures.

questions.q: In an if statement, what happens if the condition evaluates to false?
o: The controlled statement is ignored and the program continues after the conditional structure
The program terminates with an error
The condition is re-evaluated until it becomes true
questions.e: If the condition is true the statement is executed; if it is false, the statement is ignored (not executed) and the program continues right after the conditional structure.

questions.q: When an if statement needs to control more than one statement, how must those statements be grouped?
o: They are enclosed in a block using braces { }
They are written on a single line
questions.e: If more than a single statement is to be executed when the condition is true, they must be grouped into a block enclosed in braces { }.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the 'else' keyword in an if/else structure?
o: It specifies what should happen when the if condition is not fulfilled
It converts the condition to an integer
questions.e: The else keyword specifies what should happen if the condition is not fulfilled: if/else performs different actions depending on whether the condition is true or false.

questions.q: A nested if/else chain such as testing x > 0, then x < 0, then else, is typically used for what purpose?
o: To repeat a block a fixed number of times
To verify a range of values or test for multiple mutually exclusive cases
To read input from the keyboard
questions.e: if + else structures can be concatenated (nested) to verify a range of values or test multiple cases; once a condition is met, the remaining statements are skipped. The example reports whether x is positive, negative or zero.

questions.q: What is the objective of the switch statement?
o: To repeat statements while a condition holds
To check several possible constant values for an expression
questions.e: The switch statement's objective is to check several possible constant values for an expression, similar to concatenating several if/else if instructions.

questions.q: A switch statement's controlling expression must return which kind of value?
o: A bool, an enum constant, an integer type, or a character
questions.e: A switch statement's controlling expression must return a bool value, an enum constant, an integer type, or a character; this value is compared to the constant values after each case.

questions.q: What is the effect of omitting the break statement at the end of a case in a switch?
o: Execution falls through and the code for the next case is also executed
questions.e: The break statement ends the switch. Omitting it causes execution to fall through so the code for the next case is executed; deliberately omitting break allows multiple case labels to share a section of code.

questions.q: In a switch statement, when are the statements following the 'default' label executed?
o: Only if no case label matches the controlling expression
Only if break is omitted everywhere
questions.e: If no case label's constant matches the controlling expression, the statements following the default label are executed. If there is no default label, nothing happens; including a default section is considered good practice.

questions.q: For the nested-if example that classifies x, which condition is tested to report that 'x is negative'?
questions.e: The example tests if (x > 0) print positive, else if (x < 0) print negative, else print zero. The 'x is negative' branch is reached when x < 0.

questions.q: In the code fragment if (x == 100) cout << "x is 100"; what is printed when x holds the value 50?
o: Nothing is printed by this if statement
questions.e: The condition x == 100 is false when x is 50, so the controlled statement is ignored and nothing is printed by this if; the program continues after the conditional.

questions.q: Programs that are not limited to a linear sequence of instructions may do which of the following during processing?
o: Bifurcate, repeat code, or take decisions
questions.e: A program is usually not limited to a linear sequence; during processing it may bifurcate, repeat code or take decisions, which is why C++ provides control structures.

questions.q: By default, in what order are the instructions of a program without any control structures executed?
questions.e: The sequence structure means programs are executed sequentially by default, one instruction after another, unless selection or repetition structures change the flow.

questions.q: Which three repetition structures does C++ provide?
questions.e: The repetition (loop) structures in C++ are while, do/while and for.

questions.q: In a while structure, when does the loop stop repeating?
questions.e: A while loop repeats an action while some condition remains true, and it stops repeating once that condition becomes false.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a while loop and a do-while loop?
o: The do-while tests its condition at the end, so its body always executes at least once
The do-while never checks a condition
The while loop always executes at least once
The do-while can only count upward
questions.e: A do-while is similar to a while but makes its loop-continuation test at the end rather than the beginning, so the loop body executes at least once.

questions.q: What is the correct general format of a do-while structure?
questions.e: The do-while format is: do { statement } while ( condition ); the body runs, then the condition is tested, so the body always executes at least once.

questions.q: What is the correct general format of a for loop?
questions.e: The for loop format is for ( initialization; LoopContinuationTest; increment ) statement, with the three parts separated by semicolons.

questions.q: What does the loop for( int counter = 1; counter <= 10; counter++ ) cout << counter << endl; print?
questions.e: The loop initialises counter to 1 and continues while counter <= 10, incrementing each time, so it prints the integers from one to ten.

questions.q: What is the difference between pre-increment (++c) and post-increment (c++)?
o: Pre-increment changes the variable after it is used; post-increment before
Pre-increment changes the variable before it is used in the expression; post-increment changes it after
They are identical in every context
Only post-increment is valid in C++
questions.e: With pre-increment (++c) the variable is changed before it is used in the expression; with post-increment (c++) the variable is used first and changed afterward.

questions.q: If c = 5, what value does the statement cout << c++; print, and what does c become afterward?
questions.e: With post-increment, cout is executed before the increment, so it prints 5, and c then becomes 6.

questions.q: If c = 5, what does the statement cout << ++c; print?
questions.e: With pre-increment (++c), c is changed to 6 first and then printed, so the output is 6.

questions.q: What is an infinite loop, and what prevents one?
o: A loop that stops after one pass; nothing prevents it
A loop that never stops; its body should contain a line that eventually makes the condition false
A loop with no body; adding a body prevents it
A loop that runs backward; reversing it prevents it
questions.e: An infinite loop is one that never stops. To prevent it, the loop body should contain a line that will eventually cause the boolean expression to become false.

questions.q: Consider two nested for loops, the outer running i from 0 to 5 and the inner running j from 0 to 5, printing i and j together on each inner pass. What appears as the first value printed on the second output line?
questions.e: The outer loop's second iteration has i = 1, and the inner loop starts with j = 0, so the line begins with '10' (i=1, j=0) and continues 11, 12, 13, 14, 15.

questions.q: In two nested loops where the outer variable i and inner variable j each range from 0 to 5, how many pairs are printed in total?
questions.e: The outer loop runs 6 times (i from 0 to 5) and for each the inner loop runs 6 times (j from 0 to 5), giving 6 x 6 = 36 printed pairs.

questions.q: In the shopping-list pseudocode 'while there are more items on my shopping list, purchase the next item and cross it off', what plays the role of the loop-continuation condition?
o: Whether there are still more items on the list
The number of items already bought
questions.e: The while loop repeats the action while a condition remains true; here the condition is 'there are more items on my shopping list', and each pass purchases the next item and crosses it off.

questions.q: Why does swapping two variables with the code y = x; x = y; fail, and what is the fix?
o: It fails because x and y must be equal; the fix is to make them equal first
The first assignment overwrites y, so both end up equal; a temporary variable is needed to hold one value during the swap
It fails because = cannot be used on integers; the fix is to use ==
It works correctly and needs no fix
questions.e: Writing y = x; then x = y; makes both variables 3 (if x was 3), losing the original y. A temporary variable is needed: temp = x; x = y; y = temp;.

questions.q: The idea of building a program from smaller, more manageable components is described by which phrase?
questions.e: The 'divide and conquer' approach constructs a program from smaller pieces or components (modules such as functions and classes), each more manageable than the whole program.

questions.q: What is a 'local variable' in the context of functions?
o: A variable available to every function in the program
A variable known only in the function in which it is defined
A variable that never changes value
questions.e: Local variables are known only in the function in which they are defined; all variables declared in a function definition are local variables.

questions.q: Which header file must be included to use predefined mathematical functions such as sqrt?
questions.e: Predefined mathematical functions like sqrt are found in the math library, which is made available by including the header file <cmath> (and using namespace std).

questions.q: What does the statement cout << sqrt( 900.0 ); print?
questions.e: The sqrt (square root) function returns the square root of its argument, so sqrt(900.0) returns 30. All functions in the math library return a double.

questions.q: All functions in the math library (such as sqrt) return a value of which type?
questions.e: All functions in the math library return a double; for example sqrt returns the square root as a double value.

questions.q: Which of the following is a valid function argument, given that arguments may be constants, variables or expressions?
o: sqrt(4), sqrt(x) and sqrt(sqrt(x)) are all valid
questions.e: Function arguments can be constants (sqrt(4)), variables (sqrt(x)) or expressions (sqrt(sqrt(x))), so all of these forms are valid.

questions.q: What is the difference between abs(x) and fabs(x)?
o: abs returns a double from <cmath>; fabs returns an int from <cstdlib>
abs returns an int and is found in <cstdlib>; fabs returns a double and is found in <cmath>
abs works only on strings; fabs works on numbers
questions.e: abs(x) returns the absolute value as an int and is found in the library cstdlib; fabs(x) returns the absolute value as a double and is found in cmath.

questions.q: A function prototype such as int square( int ); tells the compiler what information?
o: The function's argument type(s) and its return type
The exact statements inside the function
The memory address of the function
questions.e: A function prototype tells the compiler the argument type and the return type of the function; int square( int ); means the function takes an int and returns an int.

questions.q: In a function definition, what is written as the return-value-type when the function does not return anything?
questions.e: The return-value-type is the data type of the result returned; if nothing is returned, void is used. Similarly, an empty or void parameter list indicates no arguments.

questions.q: A function 'signature' consists of which parts of the prototype?
o: The function name together with its parameters
questions.e: The function signature is the part of the prototype containing the name and the parameters, for example double maximum( double, double, double );.

questions.q: What is 'argument coercion' in a function call?
o: Forcing arguments to be of the proper type, e.g. converting int 4 to double 4.0
questions.e: Argument coercion forces arguments to be of the proper type; for example converting an int (4) to a double (4.0). Converting from double to int can truncate data, e.g. 3.4 becomes 3.

questions.q: When arguments are passed 'by value', what is actually given to the function?
o: Copies of the values of the variables, not the variables themselves
The memory addresses of the variables
questions.e: When calling a function with parameters passed by value, what is passed are copies of the values, never the variables themselves, so the originals cannot be changed by the function.

questions.q: How is a parameter declared so that it is passed by reference?
o: By writing const before the type
By placing an ampersand & after the data type, e.g. void myFunction( int &data )
By placing an asterisk * before the name
questions.e: To pass by reference, an ampersand & is placed after the data type in the prototype, e.g. void myFunction( int &data ); this creates an alias so the original variable can be changed.

questions.q: In the program that calls duplicate(x, y, z) with x=1, y=3, z=7, where duplicate multiplies each reference parameter by 2, what is the output?
questions.e: Because a, b and c are passed by reference (int&), doubling them changes the originals, so x becomes 2, y becomes 6 and z becomes 14.

questions.q: What is the main difference between call-by-value and call-by-reference?
o: Call-by-value can change the original data; call-by-reference cannot
Call-by-value passes a copy so the original is unchanged; call-by-reference lets the function access and change the original
Both always change the original data
questions.e: Call-by-value passes a copy of the data, so changes to the copy do not affect the original (preventing side effects). Call-by-reference lets the function directly access and change the original data.

questions.q: In the function definition int divide (int a, int b=2), what does the '=2' provide?
o: A default value used for b if the argument is left blank in the call
questions.e: b=2 sets a default parameter value, used if the corresponding argument is left blank when calling the function. So divide(12) uses b=2 and returns 6, while divide(20,4) returns 5.

questions.q: For int divide (int a, int b=2) that returns a/b, what does the call divide(12) return?
questions.e: Because the second argument is omitted, the default b=2 is used, so the function returns 12/2 = 6.

questions.q: A recursive function is one that does what?
o: Calls itself, breaking a problem into smaller problems until a base case is reached
questions.e: Recursive functions call themselves. If the problem is not the base case, it is broken into smaller problem(s) with new recursive calls that converge toward the base case, which is eventually solved.

questions.q: In computing factorial recursively, what is the base case?
questions.e: The recursive relationship is n! = n * (n - 1)!, and the base case is 1! = 0! = 1, at which the recursion stops.

questions.q: In the factorial program, if the user types 9, what does the program print as 9!?
questions.e: The recursive factorial computes 9! = 9*8*7*6*5*4*3*2*1 = 362880, which the program prints as '9! = 362880'.

questions.q: What does function overloading allow?
o: Two functions with identical names, parameters and bodies
More than one definition for the same function name, differing in the number and/or types of parameters
A function to have no return type
questions.e: Function overloading provides more than one declaration/definition using the same function name. Overloaded functions must have different numbers of parameters and/or at least one different parameter type.

questions.q: Given overloaded functions int operate(int a, int b) returning a*b and float operate(float a, float b) returning a/b, what are the outputs of operate(5,2) and operate(5.0,2.0)?
questions.e: operate(5,2) matches the int version and returns 5*2 = 10; operate(5.0,2.0) matches the float version and returns 5.0/2.0 = 2.5.

questions.q: How is a global named constant, such as const double PI = 3.14159, made available to both main and other functions?
o: It is declared inside main only
It is declared outside any function body, before any function that uses it
It is passed by reference to every function
It is declared inside each function separately
questions.e: A global named constant is declared outside any function body (including main), before any function that uses it, so it is available to main and to the other functions such as volume.

questions.q: How is an array best defined?
o: A single memory location holding one value
A consecutive group of memory locations with the same name and type
A group of variables of different types
A function that returns many values
questions.e: An array is a consecutive (contiguous) group of memory locations that share the same name and type, whose individual elements are referenced by adding an index to the array name.

questions.q: In C++, the first element of an array is at which position (index)?
questions.e: To refer to an element you specify the array name and a position number (index), and the first element is at position 0, using the format arrayname[position number].

questions.q: Which is the correct general form for declaring an array?
questions.e: An array declaration specifies the type, the name and the number of elements in the form type arrayName[ arraySize ]; for example int c[10];.

questions.q: What does the declaration int n[ 5 ] = { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 }; do?
o: Declares an array and leaves it uninitialised
Declares a 5-element array and sets its elements to 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 using an initializer list
Declares a single integer equal to 5
questions.e: This uses an initializer list to specify each element when the array is declared, giving a 5-element array holding 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5.

questions.q: If an initializer list has fewer values than the array size, such as int n[5] = {0};, what happens to the remaining elements?
o: The rightmost (remaining) elements are set to 0
questions.e: If there are not enough initializers, the rightmost elements are set to 0. Thus int n[5] = {0}; sets every element to 0, while too many initializers cause a syntax error.

questions.q: In the declaration int n[] = { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 }; with the size omitted, how many elements does the array have?
questions.e: When the array size is omitted, the number of initializers determines the size; with 5 initializers the array has 5 elements.

questions.q: What happens when a program uses an out-of-range array index, such as writing to a[7] for an array declared int a[6]?
o: A clear error message is displayed
No warning is given; the value is written to the computed (illegal) address, possibly overwriting another variable
questions.e: Using an out-of-range index does not produce an error message. The computer calculates the address of the illegal element (e.g. a[7]) and stores the value there, which may overwrite some other variable, with no warning given.

questions.q: For an array declared int a[6], what is the valid range of index values?
questions.e: For int a[6] the index values run from 0 through 5. Using an index outside this range (such as 6 or 7) is out of range.

questions.q: Why do most compilers reject code such as cin >> number; int score[number];?
o: Because number must be a float
Because most compilers do not allow a variable to be used to declare the size of an array
questions.e: Most compilers do not allow the use of a variable to declare the size of an array, so declaring int score[number]; with a variable size is illegal on many compilers. A const value is used instead.

questions.q: What is the recommended way to specify an array's size so it can be reused throughout the program?
o: Use a plain variable that changes at run time
Use a constant, e.g. const int size = 20;, which must be initialized when declared and cannot change
questions.e: Array size can be specified with a constant variable, e.g. const int size = 20;. Constants cannot be changed and must be initialized when declared.

questions.q: In C-style string arrays, what marks the end of every string?
questions.e: Strings are arrays of characters, and all such strings end with the null character '\0'. For example char string1[] = "hello"; implicitly adds the null character, giving 6 elements.

questions.q: How many elements does the array declared as char string1[] = "hello"; occupy?
questions.e: The five letters of 'hello' plus the implicitly added null character '\0' give a total of 6 elements.

questions.q: When char string1[20]; is read with cin >> string1; and the user types 'hello there', what is stored in string1?
questions.e: cin >> stops at the first whitespace character, so only 'hello' is stored (with a null character added); the word 'there' after the space is not captured.

questions.q: How is an entire array passed to a function, for example passing myArray to myFunction?
o: By specifying the array name without brackets, e.g. myFunction( myArray, 24 );
Arrays cannot be passed to functions
questions.e: To pass an array you specify its name without brackets, e.g. myFunction( myArray, 24 ). The array size is usually also passed (though not required) so the function can iterate over the elements.

questions.q: Why are arrays effectively passed to functions 'by reference', allowing the function to modify the original data?
o: Because the compiler copies the whole array
Because the value of an array's name is the address of its first element, so the function knows where the array is stored
questions.e: The value of the name of an array is the address of its first element, so passing the name lets the function know where the array is stored and change the original memory locations. Individual array elements, however, are passed by value.

questions.q: How can a function parameter be declared so that the function cannot modify the array passed to it?
o: Declare it with the static keyword
Declare the array parameter as const, e.g. void doNotModify( const int [] );
questions.e: If an array parameter is declared const, e.g. void doNotModify( const int [] );, the function cannot modify it, and any attempt produces a compiler error.

questions.q: Which sorting method makes several passes through an array, comparing successive pairs of elements and exchanging them when they are out of order?
questions.e: Bubble sort (also called sinking sort) makes several passes through the array; successive pairs of elements are compared and exchanged if they are in the wrong order, so small elements 'bubble' to the top.

questions.q: In a bubble sort, small elements are said to do what?
questions.e: In bubble sort, small elements 'bubble' to the top of the array as successive passes exchange out-of-order pairs; the technique is also called sinking sort.

questions.q: Which search technique compares each element of an array with a key value, one after another, and is useful for small, unsorted arrays?
questions.e: Linear search compares each element of the array with the key value, starting at one end and moving to the other. It is useful for small and unsorted arrays but is inefficient because it may examine every element.

questions.q: In the linear search program, the array is filled with a[i] = 2*i and the user searches for the key 36. The program reports it was found in which element, and why is the key 37 reported as not found?
o: Element 18; because a[18] = 36, whereas no element equals 37
Element 72; because the array doubles the index
Element 0; because searching always starts at 0
questions.e: Since a[i] = 2*i, the value 36 is stored at index 18 (2*18 = 36), so it is found in element 18. No index gives 37 (all stored values are even), so 37 is reported as not found.

questions.q: A multidimensional array is best described as which of the following?
o: An array that can hold only one value
An 'array of arrays', for example a two-dimensional table of rows and columns
An array whose elements have different types
A pointer to a single integer
questions.e: Multidimensional arrays can be described as 'arrays of arrays'; a two-dimensional array is like a table of rows and columns, accessed with multiple subscripts such as a[i][j].

questions.q: For a two-dimensional array declared int b[2][2] = { {1,2},{3,4} }, what is the correct way to reference an element, and what is invalid?
o: b[0,1] is correct; b[0][1] is a syntax error
b[0][1] is correct; using commas as in b[0,1] is a syntax error
Both b[0][1] and b[0,1] work identically
questions.e: Elements are referenced with separate brackets such as b[0][1]. Referencing with commas, e.g. b[0,1], is a syntax error.

questions.q: For int array2[ 2 ][ 3 ] = { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 }; (with only five initializers), what are the values in the second row?
questions.e: The six positions are filled in order 1,2,3 then 4,5, and the missing last element defaults to 0, so the second row is 4 5 0.

questions.q: What is the reference operator & used for?
o: To obtain the address of a variable; it reads as 'address of'
questions.e: The reference operator & obtains the address that locates a variable in memory; it can be read literally as 'address of'. For example ted = &andy; assigns to ted the address of andy.

questions.q: A variable that stores a reference (address) to another variable is called what?
questions.e: A variable that stores a reference to another variable is called a pointer; pointers are said to 'point to' the variable whose reference (address) they store.

questions.q: What does the dereference operator * do when applied to a pointer?
o: Gives the address of the pointer
Gives the value stored in the variable the pointer points to; it reads as 'value pointed by'
questions.e: The dereference operator * precedes a pointer's identifier and gives direct access to the value stored in the variable it points to; it reads as 'value pointed by'.

questions.q: If a pointer 'ted' holds the address 1776, and the value stored at address 1776 is 25, what do the expressions ted and *ted represent respectively?
questions.e: The expression ted refers to the address value 1776, while *ted (dereferenced) refers to the value stored at that address, which is 25.

questions.q: Which statement correctly summarises the & and * operators?
o: & means 'value pointed by' and * means 'address of'
& means 'address of' and * means 'value pointed by'
questions.e: & is the reference operator read as 'address of', and * is the dereference operator read as 'value pointed by'.

questions.q: How is a pointer to a variable of type double declared?
questions.e: A pointer that can point to a double is declared as double *p; where the asterisk identifies p as a pointer variable.

questions.q: In the declaration int *p1, *p2, v1, v2; which identifiers are pointers?
o: Only p1 and p2 are pointers; v1 and v2 are ordinary int variables
Only v1 and v2 are pointers
questions.e: To declare multiple pointers, the asterisk must precede each pointer name, so p1 and p2 are pointers to int, while v1 and v2 are ordinary int variables.

questions.q: After the statements v1 = 0; p1 = &v1; *p1 = 42; what is the value of v1?
questions.e: p1 is made to point to v1, and *p1 = 42 stores 42 at the location p1 points to, which is v1; so v1 becomes 42, and both v1 and *p1 print 42.

questions.q: What is the difference between the pointer assignments p1 = p2; and *p1 = *p2;?
o: p1 = p2 changes which location p1 points to; *p1 = *p2 changes the value at the location p1 points to
p1 = p2 changes a value; *p1 = *p2 changes an address
questions.e: p1 = p2; changes the location that p1 points to, while *p1 = *p2; changes the value stored at the location p1 points to. Care is required to distinguish them.

questions.q: Why is the identifier of an array considered equivalent to a pointer?
o: Because arrays and pointers use different memory
Because the identifier of an array is equivalent to the address of its first element
Because arrays store addresses instead of values
Because pointers cannot point to arrays
questions.e: The identifier of an array is equivalent to the address of its first element, just as a pointer holds the address of the element it points to, so an array name and a pointer represent the same concept.

questions.q: Given int numbers[20]; and int *p; why is the assignment numbers = p; invalid even though p = numbers; is valid?
o: Because p is a constant pointer
Because an array name acts as a constant pointer, and constants cannot be assigned new values
Because numbers and p have different types
Because arrays cannot be used with pointers at all
questions.e: numbers is an array, which operates as a constant pointer, so you cannot assign a new value to it (numbers = p; is invalid). However p is an ordinary pointer, so p = numbers; is valid.

questions.q: The bracket operator [] used with arrays is also known as which operator, and how does it work?
o: The reference operator; it gives an address
The offset operator; it dereferences and adds the number in brackets to the address, so a[5] equals *(a+5)
The scope operator; it selects a namespace
The comma operator; it separates expressions
questions.e: The brackets [] act as the offset (dereference) operator: they dereference the variable they follow and add the number in brackets to the address, so a[5] = 0; is equivalent to *(a+5) = 0;.

questions.q: When declaring char * terry = "hello";, what value does terry actually contain?
o: The address of the first character of the stored string (e.g. 1702)
questions.e: terry contains the address of the first character of the memory block holding "hello" (e.g. 1702), not the character 'h' nor the string itself.

questions.q: For char * terry = "hello";, what is the value of both *(terry+4) and terry[4]?
questions.e: Both *(terry+4) and terry[4] access the fifth element of the string "hello", which is 'o'.

questions.q: Which arithmetic operations are allowed on pointers?
questions.e: Only addition and subtraction operations make sense with pointers; the other arithmetic operations are not allowed. Their behaviour also depends on the size of the data type pointed to.

questions.q: Assume char takes 1 byte, short takes 2 bytes and long takes 4 bytes, and that mychar, myshort and mylong point to addresses 1000, 2000 and 3000. After mychar++, myshort++ and mylong++, what are their new values?
questions.e: Incrementing a pointer advances it to the next element of its type, adding the type's size in bytes: mychar becomes 1001 (+1), myshort becomes 2002 (+2), and mylong becomes 3004 (+4).

questions.q: Why does adding one to a pointer not always increase its stored address by exactly one?
o: Because adding one advances the pointer to the next element of its type, so the size in bytes of that type is added
Because addition is not allowed on pointers
questions.e: When one is added to a pointer, it is made to point to the following element of the same type, so the size in bytes of the pointed type is added to the address; a short (2 bytes) advances by 2, a long (4 bytes) by 4.

questions.q: Because ++ has higher precedence than *, the expression *p++ is equivalent to which of the following?
questions.e: Since ++ has greater precedence than *, *p++ is equivalent to *(p++): the pointer p is incremented, but the whole expression evaluates to the value pointed to by the original address (postfix).

questions.q: How does (*p)++ differ from *p++?
o: (*p)++ increases the value pointed to by p, leaving the pointer unchanged, whereas *p++ advances the pointer
(*p)++ advances the pointer, while *p++ changes the value
questions.e: In (*p)++ the value pointed to by p is increased by one and the pointer p itself is not modified, unlike *p++ which increments the pointer.

questions.q: How is a pointer-to-a-pointer declared in C++?
o: By adding an asterisk for each level of reference, e.g. char ** c;
Pointers to pointers are not allowed
questions.e: C++ allows pointers that point to other pointers; you add an asterisk for each level of reference, e.g. char a; char * b; char ** c;.

questions.q: What is special about a 'void pointer'?
o: It can only point to integers
It can point to a value of any data type, but the data it points to cannot be directly dereferenced
It cannot be assigned any address
questions.e: A void pointer points to a value that has no type, so it can point to any data type; the trade-off is that the data it points to cannot be directly dereferenced, since there is no type to dereference to.

questions.q: What is a null pointer?
o: A pointer that points to any valid memory address
A pointer holding a special value (the result of casting integer 0) that indicates it points to nowhere
A pointer that points to another pointer
questions.e: A null pointer is a regular pointer holding a special value, obtained by casting the integer 0 to a pointer type (e.g. p = 0;), indicating it does not point to any valid reference or address.

questions.q: How does a null pointer differ from a void pointer?
o: A null pointer represents pointing to 'nowhere', whereas a void pointer can point somewhere but without a specific type
A void pointer always equals zero
A null pointer can point to any data type
questions.e: A null pointer is a value any pointer may take to show it points 'nowhere', while a void pointer is a special type of pointer that can point somewhere but without a specific type; the two should not be confused.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a structure (struct) in C?
o: To repeat a block of code
To group together related data into a single composite variable
questions.e: Structures group together related data into a composite variable, which clarifies the code, simplifies passing the data to functions as a single unit, and increases the locality of the code.

questions.q: How does a structure differ from an array in terms of element size and access?
o: A structure's elements must all be the same size and are accessed by numerical index
A structure's elements may be of varying size and each is accessed by a tag (member name) rather than a numerical index
A structure can hold only one element
A structure is accessed only through pointers
questions.e: A structure is like an array whose elements can be of varying size; because the elements differ, each is given a tag (member name) and accessed by that name rather than by a numerical index.

questions.q: In memory, how are the elements of a structure arranged?
o: In reverse of their definition order
In the same order as they are defined in the struct definition
questions.e: The elements of a structure are arranged in memory in the same order as they are defined in the struct definition; each element is accessed via the structure's starting address plus that element's relative offset.

questions.q: How many members does the following structure have: struct Date { int day; int month; int year; };?
questions.e: The Date structure has three members: day, month and year, each of which is an int.

questions.q: Consider struct StudentInfo { int Id; int age; char Gender; double CGA; };. How many members does it have and are they the same type?
o: 4 members, all of the same type
5 members, all of the same type
questions.e: StudentInfo has four members (Id, age, Gender, CGA) of different types: two ints, a char and a double.

questions.q: The structure struct StudentGrade { char Name[15]; char Course[9]; int Lab[5]; int Homework[3]; int Exam[2]; }; is notable because its five members are of what kind?
questions.e: The StudentGrade structure has five members that are of different array types: two char arrays and three int arrays of differing sizes.

questions.q: The declaration struct motor M[25]; does what?
o: Declares a single struct motor variable
Declares a 25-element array of struct motor, allocating storage for 25 motors
Declares a pointer to struct motor
questions.e: struct motor M[25]; declares a 25-element array of struct motor, allocating 25 units of storage, each big enough to hold the data of one motor.

questions.q: Given struct motor p; how is the 'volts' member of p accessed?
questions.e: For an ordinary structure variable, members are accessed with the dot operator: p.volts is the voltage, p.amps the amperage, and so on.

questions.q: Given struct motor q[10]; how is the speed (rpm) of the ith motor accessed?
questions.e: For an array of structures, an element's member is accessed by indexing then using the dot operator: q[i].rpm is the speed of the ith motor and q[i].volts its voltage.

questions.q: If p is a pointer to a structure, the clumsy notation (*p).volts can be replaced by which preferred notation?
questions.e: Because (*p).member is clumsy to type and requires matching parentheses, the special notation p->member was invented, where p is a pointer to the structure; so (*p).volts becomes p->volts.

questions.q: Which operation copies one entire structure into another of the same type?
questions.e: Structures support copy/assignment directly: given struct motor p, q; the statement p = q; copies the whole structure q into p.

questions.q: Given struct motor p; and struct motor *s; how is the address of p assigned to the pointer s?
questions.e: The address of a structure variable is obtained with the & operator: s = &p; makes s point to p, after which members can be accessed as s->amps.

questions.q: Why is it generally more efficient to pass a pointer to a large structure to a function rather than the structure itself?
o: Because passing the structure by value copies the whole structure, whereas passing a pointer avoids copying the entire structure
Because a pointer changes the structure's type
questions.e: Passing an argument by value copies the whole structure, so for a large structure it is generally more efficient to pass a pointer than to copy the entire structure.

questions.q: The structure struct BankAccount { char Name[15]; int AcountNo[10]; double balance; Date Birthday; }; illustrates that a structure's members can include which kinds of types?
o: Simple types, array types, and other structure types
questions.e: The BankAccount structure has simple (double balance), array (char Name[15], int AcountNo[10]) and structure (Date Birthday) members, showing that a structure can contain simple, array and structure types.
